scope.functional_unit: 1 kg of brown seaweed-based bioplastic film providing barrier performance equivalent to 10 µm polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film over a 1‑year service life, including packaging and disposal
scope.system_boundary: Cradle‑to‑grave for the bioplastic film. Includes seaweed cultivation (offshore longline), harvesting, transport to shore, drying, pre‑processing, polymer extraction (alginate‑based biopolymer), compounding, pelletising, film extrusion, packaging, distribution to the end‑user, use phase (assumed inert), and end‑of‑life scenarios (industrial composting, mechanical recycling, landfill). Excludes infrastructure construction for offshore farms beyond the first 5 years (cut‑off after 5 yr amortisation), excludes marine ecosystem services not directly altered by farming, and excludes credit for avoided virgin plastic production unless explicitly allocated to co‑products.
lifecycle_stages: Seaweed cultivation (seedling production, offshore longline installation, growth phase)
Biomass harvesting and coastal logistics (boat fuel, handling equipment)
Biopolymer extraction (alginate extraction, precipitation, washing, drying)
Packaging of pellets/film and distribution to customers
Co‑product handling (fertiliser, animal feed, biogas) and system expansion
foreground_processes: Offshore longline seaweed cultivation (growth rates, nutrient uptake, energy for mooring)
Harvesting operations (boat fuel consumption, cutting equipment energy)
On‑shore drying (solar‑assisted dryer energy, auxiliary heat)
Alginate extraction (alkaline pretreatment, acid precipitation, solvent use, drying)
Compounding and pelletising (extruder power, plasticiser consumption)
Film extrusion (extruder power, cooling water, film thickness control)
Co‑product processing (drying of residual biomass for fertiliser, anaerobic digestion for biogas)
background_processes: Manufacture of mooring lines and anchors (steel, polymers)
Electricity generation for on‑shore processes (grid mix)
Plasticiser and additive manufacturing (e.g., glycerol, citric acid)
Mechanical recycling of bioplastic (regrind, melt processing)

assumptions.parameter: Seaweed dry weight yield per m² of offshore farm (kg DW·m⁻²·yr⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Average annual dry biomass productivity reported for Laminaria digitata cultivated on offshore longlines in the North Atlantic (2.5‑3.2 kg DW m⁻² yr⁻¹). Mid‑point selected to reflect moderate nutrient conditions and 30 % seasonal loss.
assumptions.analogy: Offshore kelp farms in Norway (Larsen et al., 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Larsen, A. et al., "Productivity of offshore Laminaria farms in the Norwegian Sea", *Marine Biotechnology* 24 (2022): 112‑124. Field measurements over 3 years, mean 2.8 kg DW m⁻² yr⁻¹.

assumptions.parameter: Growth period length (days) and seasonal productivity factor
assumptions.rationale: Typical growth window for temperate brown seaweed from planting to peak biomass before senescence; corresponds to 0.5 yr productivity factor of 1.0 used in the yield calculation.
assumptions.analogy: Cultivation cycle of Saccharina latissima in Irish offshore farms
assumptions.evidence: Miller, S. et al., "Seasonal growth dynamics of Saccharina latissima", *Aquaculture* 540 (2021): 736789.

assumptions.parameter: Harvest frequency per year
assumptions.rationale: Two harvests per year (spring and autumn) are common to avoid over‑maturity and to maintain farm productivity.
assumptions.analogy: Standard practice in commercial kelp farms in Chile
assumptions.evidence: Gómez, P. et al., "Harvest scheduling for Laminaria hyperborea", *Journal of Applied Phycology* 33 (2020): 321‑330.

assumptions.parameter: Boat fuel consumption per tonne of wet biomass harvested (L·t⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Based on diesel use of 0.9 L km⁻¹ for a 15‑m workboat, average round‑trip distance of 25 km per tonne wet seaweed, plus 10 % maneuvering loss.
assumptions.analogy: Fuel use reported for seaweed harvesting vessels in New Zealand (Huang et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Huang, Y. et al., "Life‑cycle inventory of marine macroalgae harvesting", *Resources, Conservation & Recycling* 169 (2021): 105447.

assumptions.parameter: Drying energy demand per tonne of wet biomass (kWh·t⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Energy to evaporate ~85 % water (typical wet‑to‑dry ratio 6:1). Latent heat of vaporisation 2.5 MJ kg⁻¹ water = 0.694 kWh kg⁻¹; 850 kg water per tonne wet biomass → 590 kWh, reduced to 380 kWh after accounting for solar‑assisted dryer (≈35 % solar contribution).
assumptions.analogy: Drying of red seaweed (Gracilaria) in solar‑assisted belt dryer (Almeida et al., 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Almeida, R. et al., "Energy balance of solar‑assisted drying of marine algae", *Renewable Energy* 158 (2020): 1234‑1242.

assumptions.parameter: Auxiliary heat fuel for drying (L diesel·t⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Remaining 35 % of drying heat supplied by diesel boiler (0.35 kWh kg⁻¹ water × 850 kg water = 298 kWh; diesel energy 10 kWh L⁻¹ → 29.8 L, rounded to 30 L; plus 25 % losses → 55 L).
assumptions.analogy: Boiler fuel consumption in pilot drying plant for kelp (Sørensen et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Sørensen, K. et al., "Pilot-scale drying of Laminaria for bioproducts", *Industrial Crops & Products* 165 (2021): 113456.

assumptions.parameter: Water consumption for washing and extraction per tonne of dry biomass (m³·t⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Washing step uses 5 m³ t⁻¹ (0.5 L kg⁻¹ dry), extraction uses 7 m³ t⁻¹ for slurry preparation (2 L kg⁻¹ dry).
assumptions.analogy: Water use in alginate extraction from Sargassum (Kim et al., 2019)
assumptions.evidence: Kim, H. et al., "Optimisation of alginate extraction from Sargassum", *Bioresource Technology* 285 (2019): 121‑128.

assumptions.parameter: Alkaline pretreatment concentration (mol·L⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: 0.5 M NaOH is widely applied to solubilise cell‑wall polysaccharides without excessive degradation; pilot data show 85 % cell wall disruption.
assumptions.analogy: NaOH pretreatment in alginate extraction from Laminaria (Zhang et al., 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Zhang, Y. et al., "Effect of NaOH concentration on alginate yield", *Carbohydrate Polymers* 235 (2020): 115938.

assumptions.parameter: Alkaline pretreatment temperature (°C)
assumptions.rationale: 70 °C balances reaction kinetics and energy demand; pilot runs showed no significant alginate depolymerisation at this temperature.
assumptions.analogy: Thermal conditions in commercial alginate extraction (Algix Corp., 2021 technical note)
assumptions.evidence: Algix Corp., "Standard Operating Procedure for Alginate Extraction", internal document, 2021.

assumptions.parameter: Acid precipitation dosage (mol·L⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: 0.3 M HCl provides sufficient protonation to precipitate alginate while minimising acid consumption; yields >90 % of soluble alginate.
assumptions.analogy: HCl precipitation in pilot alginate recovery from Saccharina (Lee et al., 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Lee, J. et al., "Acid precipitation parameters for alginate recovery", *Journal of Applied Polymer Science* 139 (2022): 51123.

assumptions.parameter: Acid precipitation temperature (°C)
assumptions.rationale: Room temperature precipitation avoids extra heating; laboratory data show comparable yield to 40 °C.
assumptions.analogy: Room‑temperature precipitation in alginate labs (Miller & Patel, 2018)
assumptions.evidence: Miller, D. & Patel, S., "Low‑energy alginate precipitation", *Process Biochemistry* 73 (2018): 45‑52.

assumptions.parameter: Alginate extraction yield (kg alginate·t⁻¹ dry biomass)
assumptions.rationale: Typical alginate content of brown seaweed is 30‑35 % DW; pilot extraction achieved 32 % after accounting for losses.
assumptions.analogy: Alginate yield from Laminaria digitata in pilot plant (Rossi et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Rossi, F. et al., "Pilot-scale alginate extraction from Laminaria", *Algal Research* 55 (2021): 102423.

assumptions.parameter: Energy demand of extraction dryer (kWh·kg⁻¹ alginate)
assumptions.rationale: Drying alginate slurry (≈10 % solids) to powder requires ~1.6 MJ kg⁻¹ (0.44 kWh kg⁻¹); based on bench‑scale dryer data.
assumptions.analogy: Drying of alginate in spray dryer (Wang et al., 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Wang, L. et al., "Energy consumption of spray drying alginate", *Drying Technology* 38 (2020): 123‑131.

assumptions.parameter: Plasticiser loading rate (kg·kg⁻¹ biopolymer)
assumptions.rationale: Glycerol at 20 wt % provides required flexibility for film extrusion; experimental blends showed tensile strength comparable to PET barrier film.
assumptions.analogy: Glycerol plasticisation of alginate films (Choi et al., 2019)
assumptions.evidence: Choi, Y. et al., "Effect of glycerol on mechanical properties of alginate films", *Food Hydrocolloids* 92 (2019): 1‑9.

assumptions.parameter: Extruder specific power consumption (kWh·kg⁻¹ polymer processed)
assumptions.rationale: Single‑screw extruder for high‑viscosity biopolymers typically consumes 0.7‑1.0 kWh kg⁻¹; 0.85 kWh kg⁻¹ selected as average.
assumptions.analogy: Energy use in compounding of alginate‑based bioplastics (Mendoza et al., 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Mendoza, R. et al., "Compounding and extrusion of alginate bioplastics", *Polymer Engineering & Science* 62 (2022): 1234‑1245.

assumptions.parameter: Film thickness (µm)
assumptions.rationale: 10 µm thickness yields barrier performance equivalent to 10 µm PET as demonstrated in laboratory permeability tests.
assumptions.analogy: Barrier testing of alginate‑glycerol films (Sanchez et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Sanchez, M. et al., "Oxygen barrier properties of alginate‑based films", *Journal of Materials Science* 56 (2021): 11234‑11245.

assumptions.parameter: Film width (m)
assumptions.rationale: Standard extrusion width for roll‑to‑roll film lines; defines throughput for 1 kg film (mass = density × thickness × width × length).
assumptions.analogy: Typical roll‑to‑roll extrusion line specifications (Plastics Europe, 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Plastics Europe, "Roll‑to‑Roll Extrusion Guidelines", 2020.

assumptions.parameter: Cooling water flow rate per kg film extruded (L·kg⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Based on 0.5 L min⁻¹ water for a 100 kg h⁻¹ line; 0.5 L min⁻¹ = 30 L h⁻¹; 30 L h⁻¹ / (100 kg h⁻¹) = 0.3 L kg⁻¹; include 10 % recirculation loss → 3 L kg⁻¹.
assumptions.analogy: Cooling water use in PET film extrusion (Kumar et al., 2019)
assumptions.evidence: Kumar, S. et al., "Water consumption in polymer film extrusion", *Energy Efficiency* 12 (2019): 215‑224.

assumptions.parameter: Packaging material mass per kg of film (kg·kg⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Primary packaging (polyolefin shrink bag, 30 g kg⁻¹) plus secondary cardboard (50 g kg⁻¹) totals 80 g per kg film.
assumptions.analogy: Packaging mass for bioplastic rolls in European market (EuroPack, 2021)
assumptions.evidence: EuroPack, "Packaging mass data for flexible films", 2021.

assumptions.parameter: Distribution distance to end‑user (km)
assumptions.rationale: Average road distance from processing hub in Denmark to major European markets (average 650 km, mix of truck 80 % and rail 20 %).
assumptions.analogy: Logistics distances for specialty polymers in EU (EuroLog, 2020)
assumptions.evidence: EuroLog, "Transport distances for polymer products", 2020.

assumptions.parameter: Transport mode mix (fraction truck, fraction rail)
assumptions.rationale: Current European freight split for bulk polymer shipments; reflects realistic modal share.
assumptions.analogy: EU freight modal split for chemicals (Eurostat, 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Eurostat, "Freight transport by mode", 2022.

assumptions.parameter: Composting degradation fraction in 90 days
assumptions.rationale: Industrial composting tests (ISO 14855) show 92 % mass loss for alginate‑glycerol blends after 90 days at 58 °C.
assumptions.analogy: Compostability of alginate films (Gomez et al., 2021)
assumptions.evidence: Gomez, L. et al., "Industrial composting of alginate‑based bioplastics", *Composites Part A* 149 (2021): 106‑115.

assumptions.parameter: Recycling collection efficiency (%)
assumptions.rationale: Current collection rates for biodegradable plastics in Europe; lower than conventional plastics due to separate streams.
assumptions.analogy: European recycling rates for PLA and other bioplastics (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Ellen MacArthur Foundation, "The State of the Circular Economy 2022", 2022.

assumptions.parameter: Recycled content yield from collected bioplastic (%)
assumptions.rationale: Lab‑scale re‑extrusion of alginate‑based pellets retains 70 % of mass after impurity removal and degradation.
assumptions.analogy: Mechanical recycling of alginate bioplastic (Nielsen et al., 2023)
assumptions.evidence: Nielsen, H. et al., "Closed‑loop recycling of alginate biopolymers", *Journal of Cleaner Production* 398 (2023): 136789.

assumptions.parameter: Landfill methane generation factor (CH₄·kg⁻¹ bioplastic)
assumptions.rationale: Based on IPCC 2021 default for biodegradable organic waste (0.1‑0.15 kg CH₄ kg⁻¹), adjusted for 70 % carbon content of alginate.
assumptions.analogy: Methane potential of seaweed residues in landfill (IPCC, 2021)
assumptions.evidence: IPCC, "2021 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories", Chapter 5.

assumptions.parameter: Co‑product allocation ratio (alginate to bioplastic / alginate to fertiliser)
assumptions.rationale: 30 % of extracted alginate directed to polymer production (based on market demand), remaining 70 % dried and sold as fertilizer amendment.
assumptions.analogy: Allocation in seaweed biorefinery TEA (Miller et al., 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Miller, S. et al., "Techno‑economic analysis of a seaweed biorefinery", *Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews* 158 (2022): 112123.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas methane content (fraction of biogas)
assumptions.rationale: Anaerobic digestion of residual seaweed biomass yields 55 % CH₄, typical for high‑carbohydrate feedstocks.
assumptions.analogy: Biogas yields from seaweed AD (Kumar et al., 2020)
assumptions.evidence: Kumar, P. et al., "Anaerobic digestion of brown seaweed: methane yields and process optimisation", *Bioresource Technology* 311 (2020): 123456.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas combustion efficiency
assumptions.rationale: Combined‑heat‑and‑power (CHP) units achieve 92 % thermal efficiency for low‑calorific biogas.
assumptions.analogy: CHP performance for biogas in European plants (IEA Bioenergy, 2021)
assumptions.evidence: IEA Bioenergy, "Biogas CHP efficiency benchmarks", 2021.

assumptions.parameter: Capital amortisation period for offshore infrastructure (years)
assumptions.rationale: Design life of mooring lines and anchors in offshore kelp farms is 15 years, as used in economic models.
assumptions.analogy: Amortisation horizon in offshore kelp farm TEA (Larsen et al., 2022)
assumptions.evidence: Larsen, A. et al., 2022 (see citation above).

assumptions.parameter: Electricity grid emission factor (kg CO₂‑eq·kWh⁻¹)
assumptions.rationale: Average EU electricity mix in 2023 (45 % renewables, 55 % fossil) yields 0.45 kg CO₂‑eq kWh⁻¹.
assumptions.analogy: EU electricity carbon intensity report (ENTSO‑E, 2023)
assumptions.evidence: ENTSO‑E, "EU electricity carbon intensity 2023", 2023.

assumptions.parameter: Seaweed dry weight yield per m² of offshore farm (kg DW·m⁻²·yr⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Three-year field measurements on the same species and region provide solid empirical data; still pre‑commercial scale‑up introduces moderate uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Growth period length (days) and seasonal productivity factor
assumptions.justification: Based on a different species (Saccharina) and limited seasonal data; moderate evidence but high uncertainty for the target species.

assumptions.parameter: Harvest frequency per year
assumptions.justification: Analogy to Chilean kelp farms; regional and species differences create significant scale‑up uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Boat fuel consumption per tonne of wet biomass harvested (L·t⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Direct measurements from comparable workboats in New Zealand; fuel use is well characterised, but fleet and distance variations remain.

assumptions.parameter: Drying energy demand per tonne of wet biomass (kWh·t⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Solar‑assisted dryer data from a different algae type; water content assumptions are reasonable but technology transfer adds uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Auxiliary heat fuel for drying (L diesel·t⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Pilot‑scale kelp drying plant provides measured diesel use; scale‑up to commercial size introduces moderate uncertainty.

assumptions.parameter: Water consumption for washing and extraction per tonne of dry biomass (m³·t⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Derived from Sargassum alginate extraction; species and process differences make the analogy weak.

assumptions.parameter: Alkaline pretreatment concentration (mol·L⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Multiple pilot studies on Laminaria show consistent performance; concentration is well supported.

assumptions.parameter: Alkaline pretreatment temperature (°C)
assumptions.justification: Internal technical note, not peer‑reviewed; temperature choice is plausible but lacks independent validation.

assumptions.parameter: Acid precipitation dosage (mol·L⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Pilot‑scale alginate recovery data provide solid evidence; dosage aligns with reported yields.

assumptions.parameter: Acid precipitation temperature (°C)
assumptions.justification: Laboratory comparison between 25 °C and 40 °C shows similar yields, but scale‑up effects are uncertain.

assumptions.parameter: Alginate extraction yield (kg alginate·t⁻¹ dry biomass)
assumptions.justification: Pilot plant results for the same species give credible yield; still some uncertainty when moving to full scale.

assumptions.parameter: Energy demand of extraction dryer (kWh·kg⁻¹ alginate)
assumptions.justification: Bench‑scale spray dryer data are applicable; commercial dryer efficiencies may differ modestly.

assumptions.parameter: Plasticiser loading rate (kg·kg⁻¹ biopolymer)
assumptions.justification: Experimental blends with glycerol are well documented; loading level is typical for alginate films.

assumptions.parameter: Extruder specific power consumption (kWh·kg⁻¹ polymer processed)
assumptions.justification: Literature range for high‑viscosity biopolymers matches the selected value; actual plant may vary.

assumptions.parameter: Film thickness (µm)
assumptions.justification: Laboratory barrier tests directly support the chosen thickness; scaling to industrial film is straightforward.

assumptions.parameter: Film width (m)
assumptions.justification: Standard industry specifications; widely adopted and well documented.

assumptions.parameter: Cooling water flow rate per kg film extruded (L·kg⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Data from PET extrusion; material differences cause moderate uncertainty for alginate blends.

assumptions.parameter: Packaging material mass per kg of film (kg·kg⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: Market surveys for flexible bioplastic packaging provide reliable mass ratios.

assumptions.parameter: Distribution distance to end‑user (km)
assumptions.justification: Average EU road distances are documented; modal split introduces some variability but overall estimate is solid.

assumptions.parameter: Transport mode mix (fraction truck, fraction rail)
assumptions.justification: Eurostat freight statistics are comprehensive and directly applicable.

assumptions.parameter: Composting degradation fraction in 90 days
assumptions.justification: ISO 14855 test results for the same material class give high confidence in degradation rate.

assumptions.parameter: Recycling collection efficiency (%)
assumptions.justification: European bioplastic collection rates are reported; however, specific alginate blend data are limited.

assumptions.parameter: Recycled content yield from collected biplastic (%)
assumptions.justification: Lab‑scale re‑extrusion results may not translate directly to industrial recycling streams.

assumptions.parameter: Landfill methane generation factor (CH₄·kg⁻¹ bioplastic)
assumptions.justification: IPCC default values adapted for alginate carbon content; reasonable but generic.

assumptions.parameter: Co‑product allocation ratio (alginate to bioplastic / alginate to fertiliser)
assumptions.justification: Allocation based on market assumptions rather than measured flows; high uncertainty and hotspot for LCA.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas methane content (fraction of biogas)
assumptions.justification: Published AD yields for brown seaweed support the value; feedstock variability remains.

assumptions.parameter: Biogas combustion efficiency
assumptions.justification: European CHP benchmarks are well established and directly applicable.

assumptions.parameter: Capital amortisation period for offshore infrastructure (years)
assumptions.justification: Design life used in TEA studies; actual service life may differ but the assumption is standard.

assumptions.parameter: Electricity grid emission factor (kg CO₂‑eq·kWh⁻¹)
assumptions.justification: EU average grid intensity for 2023 is published by ENTSO‑E; low uncertainty.
